volume_title: Mass Transit Launch Technologies from First Principles

chapters.title: Newton, Kepler, and Orbital Velocity

references.text: Newton, Isaac, *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, 1687. The original statement of the three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. Modern English translation: Cohen, I. B., and Whitman, A., University of California Press, 1999.
Kepler, Johannes, *Harmonices Mundi*, 1619. The original statement of the third law. Modern English translation: Aiton, E. J., Duncan, A. M., and Field, J. V., American Philosophical Society, 1997.
Huygens, Christiaan, *Horologium Oscillatorium*, 1673. The original derivation of centrifugal force in a rotating frame.

International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), *IERS Conventions (2010)*, IERS Technical Note No. 36, edited by G. Petit and B. Luzum, Verlag des Bundesamts für Kartographie und Geodäsie, Frankfurt am Main, 2010. Source for GM~E~ and ω~sidereal~.

National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, *World Geodetic System 1984: Its Definition and Relationships with Local Geodetic Systems*, NGA.STND.0036_1.0.0_WGS84, 2014. Source for R~E~ (equatorial radius).

Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013. Standard graduate text for orbital mechanics. Used as a cross-check on Kepler's Third Law numerical values.

Curtis, H. D., *Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students*, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014. Undergraduate text used as a cross-reference for derivation styles. Chapter 2 covers exactly the material of this chapter.

Bate, R. R., Mueller, D. D., and White, J. E., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics*, Dover, 1971. The classic introductory text. Chapter 1 derives all the equations of this chapter from a slightly different angle.

chapters.title: Escape Velocity and Hyperbolic Excess

references.text: Laplace, P.-S., *Exposition du Système du Monde*, 1796. First derivation of the surface escape velocity from energy considerations.

Hohmann, W., *Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper*, R. Oldenbourg, Munich, 1925. The original derivation of the minimum-energy transfer orbit and the introduction of hyperbolic departure velocities for interplanetary missions.

Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013. Chapters 1 and 2 cover escape velocity, hyperbolic trajectories, and the patched-conic approximation in standard graduate form.

Curtis, H. D., *Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students*, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014. Chapter 2 covers escape velocity; Chapter 8 covers interplanetary trajectories with worked examples for several destinations.

Bate, R. R., Mueller, D. D., and White, J. E., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics*, Dover, 1971. Chapter 1 covers conic sections; Chapter 8 covers interplanetary trajectories with the original NASA training-school style.

Battin, R. H., *An Introduction to the Mathematics and Methods of Astrodynamics*, AIAA, 1999. The definitive reference for high-precision mission design. Used as a cross-check for the heliocentric departure formulas.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration, *Solar System Dynamics*, JPL, accessed 2025. Source for Earth's mean orbital velocity (29.7847 km/s) and the Sun's standard gravitational parameter (1.32712440018 × 10²⁰ m³/s²).

Petropoulos, A. E., and Longuski, J. M., "Shape-Based Algorithm for the Automated Design of Low-Thrust, Gravity-Assist Trajectories," *Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets*, vol. 41, no. 5, 2004, pp. 787-796. Cited for mission-design context relevant to outer-solar-system trajectories.

chapters.title: Kepler's Third Law and Transfer Orbits

references.text: Hohmann, W., *Die Erreichbarkeit der Himmelskörper*, R. Oldenbourg, Munich, 1925. The original derivation of the minimum-energy transfer orbit. Hohmann was working on rocket trajectories years before any rocket capable of reaching orbit existed.

Hoelker, R. F., and Silber, R., *The Bi-Elliptical Transfer Between Co-Planar Circular Orbits*, Army Ballistic Missile Agency, Redstone Arsenal, AL, DA-TM-2-59, 1959. The original derivation of the bi-elliptic transfer and the 11.94 crossover ratio.

Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013. Chapter 6 covers two-body orbital transfers, including Hohmann, bi-elliptic, and one-tangent burn variants. The standard graduate reference.

Curtis, H. D., *Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students*, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014. Chapter 6 covers Hohmann transfers with worked examples; Chapter 8 covers interplanetary trajectories using the patched-conic method.

Bate, R. R., Mueller, D. D., and White, J. E., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics*, Dover, 1971. Chapter 3 covers orbital maneuvers including Hohmann. The classic undergraduate text from the U.S. Air Force Academy.

Battin, R. H., *An Introduction to the Mathematics and Methods of Astrodynamics*, AIAA, 1999. The definitive treatment for high-precision mission design. Chapter 6 covers transfers; Chapter 9 covers patched-conic interplanetary trajectories with full derivations.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration, *Solar System Dynamics*, JPL, accessed 2025. Source for planetary orbital periods, semi-major axes, and standard gravitational parameters used in the worked examples.

Sergeyevsky, A. B., Snyder, G. C., and Cunniff, R. A., *Interplanetary Mission Design Handbook, Volume 1, Part 2: Earth to Mars Ballistic Mission Opportunities, 1990-2005*, JPL Publication 82-43, 1983. The classic reference for actual Mars launch window data; demonstrates how the idealized Hohmann numbers translate into real mission planning.
Apollo Program Mission Reports (Apollo 8 onward), NASA, 1968-1972. Source for the actual TLI Δv of 3.05 km/s from a 185 km parking orbit, against which the 3.12 km/s computed here is cross-checked.

chapters.title: Centrifugal Excess and Hoop Stress

references.text: Birch, P., "Orbital Ring Systems and Jacob's Ladders," *Journal of the British Interplanetary Society*, vol. 35, 1982, pp. 475-497. The original technical statement of the orbital ring concept, including the hoop stress derivation in essentially the form used in this chapter.

Pearson, J., "The Orbital Ring Concept," *Acta Astronautica*, vol. 9, 1982, pp. 191-198. A parallel and slightly different formulation of the same physics, focused on the static support of the casing rather than the deployment dynamics. The mass ratio derivation differs from Birch's; this book uses the momentum-conservation derivation as the primary approach.
Forward, R. L., *Indistinguishable from Magic*, Baen, 1995. Chapter 4 includes a popularization of the orbital ring concept with cable stress numbers that match the framework in this chapter.

Yakobson, B. I., and Avouris, P., "Mechanical Properties of Carbon Nanotubes," in *Carbon Nanotubes: Synthesis, Structure, Properties, and Applications*, edited by M. S. Dresselhaus, G. Dresselhaus, and P. Avouris, Springer, 2001, pp. 287-329. The reference treatment of theoretical CNT strength used as the source for the 100 GPa SWCNT value in Table 4.1.

Bai, Y., Zhang, R., Ye, X., Zhu, Z., Xie, H., Shen, B., Cai, D., Liu, B., Zhang, C., Jia, Z., Zhang, S., Li, X., and Wei, F., "Carbon Nanotube Bundles with Tensile Strength over 80 GPa," *Nature Nanotechnology*, vol. 13, 2018, pp. 589-595. The published laboratory record for high-strength CNT bundles, supporting the trajectory toward the Vol II 25 GPa design target.

Bonnell, D., et al., "Carbon Nanotube Yarns at 14 GPa: Engineering Limit and Path to Higher Strength," referenced in Vol II Chapter 11 as the 2024 demonstrated commercial-yarn record. Citation will be finalized when Chapter 11 source pack is finalized; for now this entry is a forward placeholder.
Ashby, M. F., *Materials Selection in Mechanical Design*, 5th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2017. Source for the steel, aluminum, titanium, and conventional polymer fiber strength values in Table 4.1.

Hibbeler, R. C., *Mechanics of Materials*, 10th ed., Pearson, 2017. Standard undergraduate text for the thin-ring hoop stress derivation. Section 8.2 of that text covers the small-arc-element analysis in the same form used in Section 4.2.1 of this chapter.
Bate, R. R., Mueller, D. D., and White, J. E., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics*, Dover, 1971. Used as a cross-reference for the centrifugal excess concept and the connection to orbital velocity.

chapters.title: Earth's Atmosphere and Altitude Effects

references.text: Picone, J. M., Hedin, A. E., Drob, D. P., and Aikin, A. C., "NRLMSISE-00 Empirical Model of the Atmosphere: Statistical Comparisons and Scientific Issues," *Journal of Geophysical Research*, vol. 107, no. A12, 2002, pp. 1468-1483. The primary reference for the atmospheric density model used throughout this chapter.

U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, NASA, and United States Air Force, NOAA-S/T 76-1562, 1976. The reference document for the lower-atmosphere densities and the layer structure described in Section 5.2.

Bird, G. A., *Molecular Gas Dynamics and the Direct Simulation of Gas Flows*, Oxford University Press, 1994. The standard reference for free molecular flow drag computation, used as the source for the C~D~ ≈ 2.2 figure for cylinders.
Cook, G. E., "Satellite Drag Coefficients," *Planetary and Space Science*, vol. 13, 1965, pp. 929-946. The original work establishing the drag coefficient for satellites in free molecular flow.

Stadtmüller, M., et al., *LDEF: Spacecraft Materials in Space*, NASA Conference Publication 3257, 1994. The reference for atomic oxygen erosion yields on materials used in spacecraft, including the Kapton value of 3 × 10⁻²⁴ cm³/atom cited in Section 5.9.

Banks, B. A., de Groh, K. K., and Miller, S. K., "Low Earth Orbital Atomic Oxygen Interactions with Spacecraft Materials," *MRS Online Proceedings*, vol. 851, 2004. Updates and refinements to the LDEF erosion yield data.

Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013. Chapter 8 covers atmospheric drag in orbital mechanics, including the relationship between density variation and orbit lifetime.

King-Hele, D. G., *Theory of Satellite Orbits in an Atmosphere*, Butterworth, 1964. The classical treatment of orbital decay due to atmospheric drag, useful as background for the energy-balance arguments in Section 5.7.
Hedin, A. E., "MSIS-86 Thermospheric Model," *Journal of Geophysical Research*, vol. 92, 1987, pp. 4649-4662. The predecessor model to NRLMSISE-00, included for historical context.

Chamberlain, J. W., *Theory of Planetary Atmospheres: An Introduction to Their Physics and Chemistry*, 2nd ed., Academic Press, 1987. Textbook reference for the hydrostatic equilibrium derivation in Section 5.3.

chapters.title: J2 Perturbation, Sidereal Time, and Inclined Orbits

references.text: Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013. Chapter 9 covers Earth's non-spherical gravity field including J2 and the nodal precession derivation. Section 9.7 has the full perturbation expansion used as the primary reference for this chapter.

Kaula, W. M., *Theory of Satellite Geodesy*, Dover, 2000 (reprint of 1966 original). The classical reference for satellite-derived measurements of J2 and higher harmonics. Source for the numerical values of J2 through J6 cited in Section 6.3.

National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, *World Geodetic System 1984: Its Definition and Relationships with Local Geodetic Systems*, NGA.STND.0036_1.0.0_WGS84, 2014. The reference standard for Earth's equatorial and polar radii, flattening, and gravitational parameters.
Schaub, H., and Junkins, J. L., *Analytical Mechanics of Space Systems*, 4th ed., AIAA, 2018. Chapter 9 covers spacecraft attitude dynamics and gyroscopic precession in the form used in Section 6.6.
Curtis, H. D., *Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students*, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014. Chapter 10 covers introductory orbital perturbations including J2.

Goldstein, H., Poole, C., and Safko, J., *Classical Mechanics*, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 2002. Chapter 5 covers gyroscopic precession and Euler's equations for rigid-body rotation in the standard graduate-mechanics form.
Roy, A. E., *Orbital Motion*, 4th ed., Institute of Physics, 2005. Chapter 6 covers orbital perturbations with emphasis on the geometric interpretation used in Section 6.5.

International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), *IERS Conventions (2010)*, IERS Technical Note No. 36, Verlag des Bundesamts für Kartographie und Geodäsie, Frankfurt am Main, 2010. Reference for J2 measurements and reference frame conventions.

chapters.title: Reference Frames and the Four Cable Configurations

references.text: Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th ed., Microcosm Press, 2013. Chapter 3 covers reference frames (ECI, ECEF, LVLH, and others) in the standard form used throughout this chapter.
Schaub, H., and Junkins, J. L., *Analytical Mechanics of Space Systems*, 4th ed., AIAA, 2018. Chapter 3 covers attitude reference frames and the relationship between rotating and inertial frames.

Birch, P., "Orbital Ring Systems and Jacob's Ladders," *Journal of the British Interplanetary Society*, vol. 35, 1982, pp. 475-497. The original orbital ring paper used a prograde configuration without identifying the subsonic-zone problem. Chapter 28 of this volume will cite Birch's original derivation and explain why the present analysis chose differently.
Pearson, J., "The Orbital Ring Concept," *Acta Astronautica*, vol. 9, 1982, pp. 191-198. Pearson's parallel formulation also assumed prograde. Same forward reference applies.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration, *NASA Spaceflight Mechanics Handbook*, Glenn Research Center, NASA SP-7100, 1971. Background reference for the rotation-rate and reference-frame conventions used in this chapter.

International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), *IERS Conventions (2010)*, IERS Technical Note No. 36, Verlag des Bundesamts für Kartographie und Geodäsie, Frankfurt am Main, 2010. Source for the sidereal rate ω~E~ = 7.2921159 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s.
Curtis, H. D., *Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students*, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2014. Chapter 4 covers reference-frame transformations used in this chapter.

Ch10_Design_Review (Volume III draft), Section 10.9. The internal design-review document for Volume III contains the original four-configuration table that this chapter formalizes. The numerical values for cable mass per meter come from that document.

chapters.title: Stress, Strain, and Specific Strength

references.text: Ashby, M. F., *Materials Selection in Mechanical Design*, 5th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann, 2017. The standard reference for materials selection by figure-of-merit. Chapters 4 and 5 cover specific strength and the materials property charts used as the basis for Section 8.6 and Table 8.1.

Hibbeler, R. C., *Mechanics of Materials*, 10th ed., Pearson, 2017. Standard undergraduate textbook for stress, strain, Young's modulus, yield, ultimate, and the stress-strain curve. Section 8.2 through 8.4 of this chapter draw heavily on this reference.

Callister, W. D., and Rethwisch, D. G., *Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction*, 10th ed., Wiley, 2018. Materials-science textbook covering stress-strain behavior, fatigue, creep, and material classification.

American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM), *ASTM E8/E8M-21: Standard Test Methods for Tension Testing of Metallic Materials*, 2021. The standard test method for measuring tensile stress and strain in metals.
Toray Industries, *Carbon Fiber T1100G Data Sheet*, accessed 2025. Source for the T1100G carbon fiber strength and density values in Table 8.1.
DSM Dyneema, *Dyneema SK99 Fiber Data Sheet*, accessed 2025. Source for the UHMWPE strength and density.
Toyobo Co., *Zylon PBO Fiber Technical Information*, accessed 2025. Source for the Zylon strength and density.

Bai, Y., Zhang, R., Ye, X., Zhu, Z., Xie, H., Shen, B., Cai, D., Liu, B., Zhang, C., Jia, Z., Zhang, S., Li, X., and Wei, F., "Carbon Nanotube Bundles with Tensile Strength over 80 GPa," *Nature Nanotechnology*, vol. 13, 2018, pp. 589-595. Cited in support of the high-strength CNT bundle progress toward the Vol II design target.

Yakobson, B. I., Brabec, C. J., and Bernholc, J., "Nanomechanics of Carbon Tubes: Instabilities Beyond Linear Response," *Physical Review Letters*, vol. 76, 1996, pp. 2511-2514. Theoretical analysis of SWCNT mechanical properties cited as the source for the 100 GPa value used as the CNT theoretical maximum in Table 8.1.

Lee, C., Wei, X., Kysar, J. W., and Hone, J., "Measurement of the Elastic Properties and Intrinsic Strength of Monolayer Graphene," *Science*, vol. 321, 2008, pp. 385-388. The landmark measurement of monolayer graphene mechanical properties, source for the 130 GPa value in Table 8.1.

chapters.title: Carbon Bonding and the Allotropes of Carbon

references.text: Atkins, P., Overton, T., Rourke, J., Weller, M., Armstrong, F., and Hagerman, M., *Shriver and Atkins' Inorganic Chemistry*, 5th ed., Oxford University Press, 2010. Standard graduate-level reference for atomic structure, electronic configurations, and hybridization. Chapter 1 covers the carbon valence-bond model used in this chapter.

Pauling, L., *The Nature of the Chemical Bond*, 3rd ed., Cornell University Press, 1960. The classical reference for hybridization, σ and π bonds, and bond-energy systematics. Pauling's framework is the basis for all subsequent treatments.

Pierson, H. O., *Handbook of Carbon, Graphite, Diamond and Fullerenes*, Noyes Publications, 1993. Comprehensive reference for the carbon allotropes, properties, and synthesis methods. Source for several of the density and strength values in Table 9.1.

Lee, C., Wei, X., Kysar, J. W., and Hone, J., "Measurement of the Elastic Properties and Intrinsic Strength of Monolayer Graphene," *Science*, vol. 321, 2008, pp. 385-388. The landmark measurement of single-layer graphene mechanical properties: σ~u~ = 130 GPa, E = 1,000 GPa.

Kroto, H. W., Heath, J. R., O'Brien, S. C., Curl, R. F., and Smalley, R. E., "C₆₀: Buckminsterfullerene," *Nature*, vol. 318, 1985, pp. 162-163. The discovery paper for fullerenes; the basis for the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Iijima, S., "Helical Microtubules of Graphitic Carbon," *Nature*, vol. 354, 1991, pp. 56-58. The modern discovery of carbon nanotubes.

Novoselov, K. S., Geim, A. K., Morozov, S. V., Jiang, D., Zhang, Y., Dubonos, S. V., Grigorieva, I. V., and Firsov, A. A., "Electric Field Effect in Atomically Thin Carbon Films," *Science*, vol. 306, 2004, pp. 666-669. The first isolation of monolayer graphene; the basis for the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

McMurry, J., *Organic Chemistry*, 9th ed., Cengage Learning, 2015. Standard organic chemistry textbook. Chapter 1 covers σ and π bonds, hybridization, and bond-energy systematics. The carbon-carbon bond energies cited in Section 9.4 are from this reference.

Charlier, J.-C., Blase, X., and Roche, S., "Electronic and Transport Properties of Nanotubes," *Reviews of Modern Physics*, vol. 79, 2007, pp. 677-732. Reference treatment of CNT electronic structure, with the chirality framework that Chapter 10 will use.

chapters.title: Graphene and Carbon Nanotubes

references.text: Lee, C., Wei, X., Kysar, J. W., and Hone, J., "Measurement of the Elastic Properties and Intrinsic Strength of Monolayer Graphene," *Science*, vol. 321, 2008, pp. 385-388. The landmark direct measurement of monolayer graphene mechanical properties.

Saito, R., Dresselhaus, G., and Dresselhaus, M. S., *Physical Properties of Carbon Nanotubes*, Imperial College Press, 1998. The standard reference for CNT structure, chirality, and electronic properties. The chiral-vector and chirality-index framework of this chapter comes from this book.

Yu, M.-F., Files, B. S., Arepalli, S., and Ruoff, R. S., "Tensile Loading of Ropes of Single Wall Carbon Nanotubes and their Mechanical Properties," *Physical Review Letters*, vol. 84, 2000, pp. 5552-5555. The first direct mechanical measurements of SWCNT bundles, giving σ~u~ = 11-63 GPa.

Yakobson, B. I., Brabec, C. J., and Bernholc, J., "Nanomechanics of Carbon Tubes: Instabilities Beyond Linear Response," *Physical Review Letters*, vol. 76, 1996, pp. 2511-2514. Theoretical analysis of SWCNT mechanical properties, source for the 100 GPa theoretical limit.

Bai, Y., Zhang, R., Ye, X., Zhu, Z., Xie, H., Shen, B., Cai, D., Liu, B., Zhang, C., Jia, Z., Zhang, S., Li, X., and Wei, F., "Carbon Nanotube Bundles with Tensile Strength over 80 GPa," *Nature Nanotechnology*, vol. 13, 2018, pp. 589-595. The published record for CNT bundle strength.
Iijima, S., "Helical Microtubules of Graphitic Carbon," *Nature*, vol. 354, 1991, pp. 56-58. The modern discovery of carbon nanotubes.
Iijima, S., and Ichihashi, T., "Single-Shell Carbon Nanotubes of 1-nm Diameter," *Nature*, vol. 363, 1993, pp. 603-605. The first observation of single-wall CNT.

Bethune, D. S., Klang, C. H., de Vries, M. S., Gorman, G., Savoy, R., Vazquez, J., and Beyers, R., "Cobalt-Catalysed Growth of Carbon Nanotubes with Single-Atomic-Layer Walls," *Nature*, vol. 363, 1993, pp. 605-607. Parallel discovery of catalytic SWCNT growth.

Dresselhaus, M. S., Dresselhaus, G., and Eklund, P. C., *Science of Fullerenes and Carbon Nanotubes*, Academic Press, 1996. Foundational reference for CNT science, including the chirality framework and the mechanical-property derivations.

Charlier, J.-C., Blase, X., and Roche, S., "Electronic and Transport Properties of Nanotubes," *Reviews of Modern Physics*, vol. 79, 2007, pp. 677-732. Reference for the electronic-type classification (metallic vs semiconductor) used in Table 10.1.
DexMat Inc., *Galvorn CNT Yarn Technical Data*, accessed 2025. Source for the commercial CNT yarn strength and density values.

chapters.title: The CNT Manufacturing Gap and the Engineering Target

references.text: Endo, M., Iijima, S., and Dresselhaus, M. S., *Carbon Nanotubes*, Pergamon, 1996. Foundational reference on CNT synthesis methods, including arc discharge, laser ablation, and early CVD.

Bai, Y., Zhang, R., Ye, X., Zhu, Z., Xie, H., Shen, B., Cai, D., Liu, B., Zhang, C., Jia, Z., Zhang, S., Li, X., and Wei, F., "Carbon Nanotube Bundles with Tensile Strength over 80 GPa," *Nature Nanotechnology*, vol. 13, 2018, pp. 589-595. Behabtu, N., Young, C. C., Tsentalovich, D. E., Kleinerman, O., Wang, X., Ma, A. W. K., Bengio, E. A., ter Waarbeek, R. F., de Jong, J. J., Hoogerwerf, R. E., Fairchild, S. B., Ferguson, J. Zhang, X., Jiang, K., Feng, C., Liu, P., Zhang, L., Kong, J., Zhang, T., Li, Q., and Fan, S., "Spinning and Processing Continuous Yarns from 4-Inch Wafer Scale Super-Aligned Carbon Nanotube Arrays," *Advanced Materials*, vol. 18, 2006, pp. 1505-1510. Tsinghua group's spinnable CNT yarn method.

Ya-Li Li, Kinloch, I. A., and Windle, A. H., "Direct Spinning of Carbon Nanotube Fibers from Chemical Vapor Deposition Synthesis," *Science*, vol. 304, 2004, pp. 276-278. The original floating-catalyst CVD direct-spinning paper.

Cox, H. L., "The Elasticity and Strength of Paper and Other Fibrous Materials," *British Journal of Applied Physics*, vol. 3, 1952, pp. 72-79. The original shear-lag analysis paper, the framework used in Section 11.3.
Kelly, A., and Macmillan, N. H., *Strong Solids*, 3rd ed., Clarendon Press, 1986. Standard reference for fiber-composite shear-lag analysis.

Vilatela, J. J., Khare, R., and Windle, A. H., "The Hierarchical Structure and Properties of Multifunctional Carbon Nanotube Fibre Composites," *Carbon*, vol. 50, 2012, pp. 1227-1234. Reference treatment of CNT yarn hierarchical structure and the resulting mechanical-property model.

Zhang, R., Wen, Q., Qian, W., Su, D. S., Zhang, Q., and Wei, F., "Superstrong Ultralong Carbon Nanotubes for Mechanical Energy Storage," *Advanced Materials*, vol. 23, 2011, pp. 3387-3391. Direct measurement of long individual SWCNTs at 100 GPa range.
Bonnell, D., et al., 2024 CNT yarn record at 14 GPa (citation to be finalized in Chapter 11 source pack; placeholder for the specific milestone publication).
DexMat Inc., *Galvorn CNT Yarn Technical Data*, accessed 2025. Commercial CNT yarn properties.
BNNT, LLC (Newport News, VA), *BNNT Yarn Technical Information*, accessed 2025. Commercial BNNT yarn properties.

Chen, Y., Zou, J., Campbell, S. J., and Le Caer, G., "Boron Nitride Nanotubes: Pronounced Resistance to Oxidation," *Applied Physics Letters*, vol. 84, 2004, pp. 2430-2432. BNNT thermal stability characterization.

Cumings, J., and Zettl, A., "Mass-Production of Boron Nitride Double-Wall Nanotubes and Nanococoons," *Chemical Physics Letters*, vol. 316, 2000, pp. 211-216. Early reference for BNNT production.

Recent high-field HTS magnet demonstration relevant to the EML bearing and the LSM stator designs.

chapters.title: Charge, Current, and Coulomb's Law

references.text: Griffiths, D. J., *Introduction to Electrodynamics*, 4th ed., Pearson, 2017. Standard undergraduate electrodynamics text. Chapters 1-2 cover the material of this chapter at the level used here.
Jackson, J. D., *Classical Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed., Wiley, 1999. Graduate-level reference for the full mathematical development of electrostatics and the field equations.
Halliday, D., Resnick, R., and Walker, J., *Fundamentals of Physics*, 11th ed., Wiley, 2018. Introductory physics text used as the basis for the Coulomb's law and electric field sections.
Ohm, G. S., *Die Galvanische Kette, Mathematisch Bearbeitet*, T. H. Riemann, Berlin, 1827. The original publication of Ohm's law.
